title: What I learned making my first game with an AI coding agent (Godot, solo, I do the design)
author: MoistAssociation6443
selftext:
I am a first time developer, and I am making Ocean Road: a survival road trip that lives in a thin strip above the Windows taskbar. An old school bus carries four people across a ruined continent to the ocean while you work, and every so often a card comes up and asks you to decide something. Take a mother and her son on board, and the food for four now has to feed six. Cross a weak bridge, or lose a day going around. At night you decide who looks for supplies, who fixes the engine and who rests.

I design the game and make every decision on the cards. Almost everything else is made with AI tools, and I want to share how the pipeline works and where it broke, because that was the part I could not find much honest writing about when I started.

**Code: one step, one session, one commit**

Claude Code writes the code in Godot 4 and GDScript. I never ask it for "the next feature" in a chat. Every change is a step written as a prompt file in the repo: the goal, what must not change, and how to check the result. One step is one session and ends with one commit. When a step goes wrong, I throw the commit away and rewrite the prompt, instead of arguing with the session for an hour.

Chats are disposable, so the memory of the project lives in documents that every session reads first: a decisions log (newest on top, each decision with its reason), a roadmap, a design document, a story bible with the rules for in-game text, and a [CLAUDE.md](http://CLAUDE.md) with the architecture and code rules. The decisions log is now over 400 KB, and it is the most useful file in the project.

**Balance: bots instead of feel**

Claude Code also wrote bots that play the whole road thousands of times with different strategies, and a report that shows how many runs arrive and how many reach the mountain pass before the snow. I set the targets myself, for example that a careless player should almost never make it and a careful one usually should, and then we change one number at a time until the report agrees.

**3D: AI-written Blender scripts from generated references**

The world is low poly 3D. For each roadside object I generate a reference image, and Claude writes a Blender Python script that builds the model from it with a fixed triangle budget and only the colours from our palette. A gas station came out at about 1 400 triangles and looks right at the size of the strip. Some models are recoloured from third party packs.

**Images and text**

The hero portraits, some backgrounds and the billboard posters are AI generated. The text on the cards is drafted with AI and then edited by me against written style rules.

**What did not work**

My first long playtest was boring. The bots said the game was balanced, but two hours in the background nothing made me look down. Bots can measure difficulty, but they cannot tell you that something is dull. Only playing it can.

Buildings were beyond the Blender script approach. Houses never looked good, and a round of 26 models for places along the road came out badly too. I removed every house from the scene and kept the road itself: gas stations, billboards, power line pylons, skyscrapers far on the horizon.

Two sessions overwrote the decisions log and quietly lost entries. Now every prompt says to read the file again right before editing it and to change as little as possible.

The interface drifted into technical documentation, with arrows, abbreviations and numbers for everything. I had to write a rule against it: full sentences in the tone of a travel journal, and numbers only for what the player actually counts.

The first drafts of the dialogue had an obvious AI sound, with short chopped sentences and long dashes everywhere. Fixing the voice took more rounds than any piece of code.

**What I would tell someone starting the same way**

The agent is fast at building and weak at judging. It will happily make exactly what you asked for, so most of your work is deciding what to ask for and then playing the result. Small steps with a check at the end matter more than clever prompts, and anything important has to live in a file, not in a conversation.

**Full AI disclosure**

Code: written by Claude Code under my direction. Text: drafted with AI, edited by me. Images: hero portraits, some backgrounds and the billboard posters are AI generated. 3D: models built from AI-written Blender scripts, plus some recoloured third party models. Sound: the demo uses sounds and music by human artists from Pixabay and Sonniss, and the engine sound is synthesised in code. The design and every choice on the cards are mine.

The game will be sold on Steam later. Right now there is a free Windows demo with the first two of five regions, about one working day in the background: [https://evg-fromspace.itch.io/ocean-road](https://evg-fromspace.itch.io/ocean-road)

For those of you making games with AI tools: how do you keep the in-game text from sounding generated? That is the part I am still least happy with.
